title: Agricultural Economics
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 300L Agricultural Economics course: basic economic concepts, demand and supply, production economics, elasticity, cost/revenue analysis, agricultural marketing and pricing, farm finance/credit, and agricultural policy fundamentals.

questions.question: Economics is generally defined as the study of what?
options: How society allocates scarce resources among unlimited competing wants
How to grow crops using modern irrigation techniques
The biology of farm animals
The chemistry of soil nutrients
questions.correct_answer: How society allocates scarce resources among unlimited competing wants
questions.explanation: Economics studies how individuals and societies make choices to allocate limited (scarce) resources to satisfy unlimited human wants.

questions.question: In economics, 'scarcity' refers to what fundamental condition?
options: Resources being limited relative to the unlimited wants they must satisfy
A temporary shortage caused only by poor weather
The complete absence of any resources
A situation that only occurs in developing countries
questions.correct_answer: Resources being limited relative to the unlimited wants they must satisfy
questions.explanation: Scarcity is the basic economic problem arising because resources (land, labour, capital) are finite while human wants are effectively unlimited, forcing choices.

questions.question: The 'opportunity cost' of choosing to plant maize on a plot of land is best described as what?
options: The value of the next best alternative crop forgone, such as cassava
The total revenue earned from selling the maize
The cost of fertiliser applied to the maize
Zero, since no money was spent
questions.correct_answer: The value of the next best alternative crop forgone, such as cassava
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative that must be given up when a choice is made -- here, the benefit of the next-best crop that could have been planted instead.

questions.question: Which four factors of production are traditionally recognised in economic analysis of agriculture?
options: Land, labour, capital, and management (entrepreneurship)
Seeds, fertiliser, pesticide, and water only
Rainfall, sunlight, temperature, and soil pH
Tractors, ploughs, silos, and barns only
questions.correct_answer: Land, labour, capital, and management (entrepreneurship)
questions.explanation: The classical factors of production are land, labour, capital, and management/entrepreneurship, which combine to produce goods and services including farm output.

questions.question: According to the law of demand, if the price of a commodity rises while other factors remain constant, what typically happens to the quantity demanded?
options: Quantity demanded decreases
Quantity demanded increases
Quantity demanded remains exactly unchanged
Quantity demanded becomes negative
questions.correct_answer: Quantity demanded decreases
questions.explanation: The law of demand states an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, ceteris paribus: as price rises, buyers demand less of the good.

questions.question: According to the law of supply, as the price of a commodity rises, what generally happens to the quantity supplied by producers?
options: Quantity supplied increases
Quantity supplied decreases
Quantity supplied stays fixed regardless of price
Supply disappears entirely
questions.correct_answer: Quantity supplied increases
questions.explanation: The law of supply describes a direct relationship between price and quantity supplied: higher prices generally incentivise producers to supply more of a good.

questions.question: Market equilibrium price is determined at the point where what occurs?
options: Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
Total demand is zero
Total supply is zero
Government fixes the price by decree
questions.correct_answer: Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
questions.explanation: Equilibrium price is where the demand and supply curves intersect, i.e. the price at which the quantity buyers want to purchase equals the quantity sellers want to sell.

questions.question: A bumper harvest of tomatoes causing a glut and sharp fall in market price is best explained by what?
options: A rightward shift in supply against relatively unchanged demand
A leftward shift in demand only
Government-imposed price controls
An increase in consumer income only
questions.correct_answer: A rightward shift in supply against relatively unchanged demand
questions.explanation: A bumper harvest increases the quantity of tomatoes available at every price (a rightward supply shift); with demand relatively stable, the market-clearing price falls.

questions.question: Price elasticity of demand measures what?
options: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price
The total revenue earned by a firm
The absolute change in price only
The cost of production per unit
questions.correct_answer: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand quantifies how much quantity demanded changes in percentage terms in response to a percentage change in price.

questions.question: Staple foods such as garri or rice in Nigeria tend to have what type of price elasticity of demand, since consumers still need to buy them even when prices rise?
options: Relatively inelastic demand
Perfectly elastic demand
Infinite elasticity
Negative infinite elasticity
questions.correct_answer: Relatively inelastic demand
questions.explanation: Staple foods are necessities with few substitutes, so quantity demanded changes proportionally less than price changes, making demand relatively inelastic.

questions.question: If a 10% increase in the price of a good leads to a 20% decrease in quantity demanded, the demand is said to be what?
options: Elastic
Inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unitary elastic
questions.correct_answer: Elastic
questions.explanation: Because the percentage change in quantity demanded (20%) exceeds the percentage change in price (10%), the elasticity coefficient exceeds 1 in absolute value, indicating elastic demand.

questions.question: The 'law of diminishing marginal returns' in agricultural production states what?
options: Beyond a certain point, adding more of a variable input to a fixed input yields progressively smaller increases in output
Output always increases proportionally with any input increase forever
Fixed costs decrease as production increases
Total cost always equals total revenue at every output level
questions.correct_answer: Beyond a certain point, adding more of a variable input to a fixed input yields progressively smaller increases in output
questions.explanation: The law of diminishing returns describes how, holding some inputs fixed (e.g. land), successive equal increases in a variable input (e.g. fertiliser) eventually produce smaller and smaller additional output.

questions.question: In production economics, 'total product' refers to what?
options: The total quantity of output produced from a given combination of inputs
The revenue earned from selling one unit of output
The additional output from one more unit of input
The average cost of production per unit
questions.correct_answer: The total quantity of output produced from a given combination of inputs
questions.explanation: Total product (TP) is the overall physical output obtained from a specified quantity of inputs used in the production process.

questions.question: 'Marginal product' of an input is defined as what?
options: The additional output produced by using one more unit of that input, holding other inputs constant
The total output divided by total cost
The price paid per unit of input
The fixed cost of production
questions.correct_answer: The additional output produced by using one more unit of that input, holding other inputs constant
questions.explanation: Marginal product (MP) measures the change in total output resulting from a one-unit increase in a variable input, other inputs held fixed.

questions.question: Fixed costs in a farm business are best described as costs that do what?
options: Remain constant regardless of the level of output produced, such as land rent
Vary directly and proportionally with output, such as seed and fertiliser
Are always zero at the start of production
Disappear once production begins
questions.correct_answer: Remain constant regardless of the level of output produced, such as land rent
questions.explanation: Fixed costs (e.g. land rent, depreciation on equipment) do not change with the level of output in the short run, unlike variable costs which rise and fall with production.

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical example of a variable cost in crop production?
options: Cost of seeds and fertiliser applied
Annual land tax paid regardless of planting
Depreciation on a tractor not currently in use
Interest on a long-term farm mortgage
questions.correct_answer: Cost of seeds and fertiliser applied
questions.explanation: Seed and fertiliser expenses vary directly with the area planted and the level of input use, making them classic variable costs, unlike fixed costs such as land tax.

questions.question: Total cost (TC) in production economics is calculated as what?
options: Total fixed cost plus total variable cost
Total revenue minus total fixed cost
Average cost multiplied by fixed cost only
Marginal cost divided by output
questions.correct_answer: Total fixed cost plus total variable cost
questions.explanation: Total cost is the sum of total fixed costs (which do not vary with output) and total variable costs (which do vary with output).

questions.question: A farmer's gross margin is calculated as what?
options: Total revenue minus total variable costs
Total revenue minus total fixed costs only
Total variable cost minus total fixed cost
Total revenue plus total cost
questions.correct_answer: Total revenue minus total variable costs
questions.explanation: Gross margin subtracts only the variable costs attributable to an enterprise from its revenue, making it a common short-run measure for comparing farm enterprises.

questions.question: A farmer sells 500 bags of maize at N8,000 per bag; total variable costs were N2,500,000 and total fixed costs were N500,000. What is the net farm income (profit)?
The break-even point in farm production is the output level at which what occurs?
options: Total revenue exactly equals total cost, so profit is zero
Total revenue is at its maximum possible value
Marginal cost equals zero
Fixed costs are eliminated entirely
questions.correct_answer: Total revenue exactly equals total cost, so profit is zero
questions.explanation: At the break-even point, total revenue covers total cost exactly, meaning the farmer neither makes a profit nor incurs a loss.

questions.question: Agricultural marketing is best defined as what?
options: All the activities involved in moving farm products from producer to final consumer
Only the act of a farmer selling produce at the farm gate
The process of growing crops using improved seed
The government's regulation of land ownership
questions.correct_answer: All the activities involved in moving farm products from producer to final consumer
questions.explanation: Agricultural marketing encompasses assembling, grading, storage, transportation, processing, distribution, and sale of farm produce from the point of production to the final consumer.

questions.question: The difference between the price a consumer pays for a farm product and the price the farmer receives for it is known as what?
options: Marketing margin
Gross margin
Net farm income
Opportunity cost
questions.correct_answer: Marketing margin
questions.explanation: The marketing margin captures the costs and profits of intermediaries (transport, storage, processing, trading) between the farm gate and the final consumer price.

questions.question: Which of the following is a major marketing function classified as a 'physical function'?
options: Storage and transportation of produce
Price negotiation between buyer and seller
Provision of market information
Risk-bearing by traders
questions.correct_answer: Storage and transportation of produce
questions.explanation: Physical marketing functions involve the actual handling of goods, such as storage, transportation, processing, and packaging, as distinct from exchange functions like buying/selling.

questions.question: A major characteristic of agricultural markets in many developing countries, including Nigeria, that distinguishes them from markets for manufactured goods is what?
options: Seasonality and perishability of produce, causing price fluctuations
Perfectly uniform prices throughout the year
Complete absence of intermediaries
Guaranteed fixed prices set permanently by farmers
questions.correct_answer: Seasonality and perishability of produce, causing price fluctuations
questions.explanation: Agricultural output is often seasonal and perishable, leading to gluts at harvest (low prices) and scarcity in off-season (high prices), unlike many manufactured goods.

questions.question: Why do agricultural commodity prices typically fall sharply immediately after harvest season in Nigeria?
options: Supply increases sharply while demand and storage capacity remain relatively limited
Demand for food always rises at harvest time
Government always sets a fixed low price after harvest
Farmers stop producing entirely after harvest
questions.correct_answer: Supply increases sharply while demand and storage capacity remain relatively limited
questions.explanation: At harvest, a large volume of produce floods the market simultaneously; with limited storage and processing capacity, this surplus supply drives prices down until stocks are absorbed.

questions.question: Agricultural credit is important to farmers mainly because it helps address what challenge?
options: The gap between when farm inputs must be paid for and when farm produce generates income
The need to permanently avoid selling any produce
The elimination of weather-related production risk
The requirement to pay import duties on farm produce
questions.correct_answer: The gap between when farm inputs must be paid for and when farm produce generates income
questions.explanation: Farming has a production cycle where inputs (seed, fertiliser, labour) must be financed months before revenue from harvest is realised; credit bridges this timing gap.

questions.question: A farm cooperative society primarily benefits its members by doing what?
options: Pooling resources for bulk input purchase, credit access, and collective marketing bargaining power
Eliminating the need for farmers to produce any crops
Setting global commodity prices unilaterally
Replacing the need for government agricultural policy entirely
questions.correct_answer: Pooling resources for bulk input purchase, credit access, and collective marketing bargaining power
questions.explanation: Cooperatives allow smallholder farmers to achieve economies of scale in input purchase, access credit collectively, and gain stronger bargaining power when marketing produce.

questions.question: In economics, what does 'monopoly' describe in a market?
options: A market structure with a single seller controlling the supply of a good with no close substitutes
A market with many small sellers and identical products
A situation where price is always below cost
A market where only the government can buy goods
questions.correct_answer: A market structure with a single seller controlling the supply of a good with no close substitutes
questions.explanation: A monopoly exists when a single firm is the sole supplier of a good or service, giving it significant control over price due to the absence of close substitutes.

questions.question: Which market structure, common for many raw agricultural commodities like maize or tomatoes sold by numerous smallholders, features many buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, and no single participant able to influence price?
options: Perfect competition
Monopoly
Monopsony
Oligopoly
questions.correct_answer: Perfect competition
questions.explanation: Perfect competition is characterised by many small producers selling a homogeneous product, each acting as a price taker because no single seller can influence the market price.

questions.question: A 'monopsony' in an agricultural market describes a situation where what occurs?
options: There is a single dominant buyer facing many sellers of a farm product
There are many buyers and many sellers
There is a single seller facing many buyers
Government sets both buying and selling prices
questions.correct_answer: There is a single dominant buyer facing many sellers of a farm product
questions.explanation: Monopsony is the buyer-side mirror of monopoly: a single (or dominant) buyer can influence the price paid to numerous smaller sellers, as sometimes seen with a sole processing company buying a raw commodity from many farmers.

questions.question: Land tenure systems in Nigeria historically based on communal or family ownership, where individuals have use-rights rather than full private ownership, can create what challenge for agricultural investment?
options: Reduced incentive for long-term investment due to insecure or fragmented land rights
Guaranteed unlimited land for every farmer at no cost
Automatic access to formal bank credit for every landholder
Elimination of any need for land use planning
questions.correct_answer: Reduced incentive for long-term investment due to insecure or fragmented land rights
questions.explanation: Where land rights are insecure, communally held, or fragmented into small plots, farmers may be reluctant to make long-term investments (e.g. irrigation, tree crops) or may lack collateral for credit.

questions.question: A government policy of subsidising fertiliser prices for farmers is intended primarily to achieve what economic effect?
options: Lower the effective input cost to encourage higher fertiliser use and production
Increase the market price of fertiliser to farmers
Reduce total agricultural output deliberately
Transfer land ownership from farmers to the government
questions.correct_answer: Lower the effective input cost to encourage higher fertiliser use and production
questions.explanation: Input subsidies reduce the price farmers pay for fertiliser, aiming to increase adoption and use, which in turn is expected to raise yields and total production.

questions.question: What is the main economic rationale for a government imposing a tariff (import duty) on imported rice?
options: To make imported rice more expensive relative to local rice, protecting domestic producers
To make imported rice cheaper than local rice
To eliminate all rice consumption in the country
To subsidise foreign rice farmers
questions.correct_answer: To make imported rice more expensive relative to local rice, protecting domestic producers
questions.explanation: Import tariffs raise the domestic price of imported goods, which can protect local producers from cheaper foreign competition, though it may raise prices for consumers.

questions.question: In farm business analysis, what does 'return on investment' (ROI) measure?
options: The profitability of an investment relative to the amount of capital invested
The total physical yield of a crop per hectare
The number of workers employed on the farm
The total land area under cultivation
questions.correct_answer: The profitability of an investment relative to the amount of capital invested
questions.explanation: ROI expresses the net gain from an investment as a percentage of the capital invested, allowing comparison of the profitability of different farm investments.

questions.question: If a good's demand rises whenever consumer income rises, that good is classified in economics as what type of good?
options: Normal good
Inferior good
Giffen good
Free good
questions.correct_answer: Normal good
questions.explanation: A normal good is one for which demand increases as consumer income increases; most food staples behave this way up to a point, unlike inferior goods whose demand falls as income rises.
